extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers, and policymakers interested in advertising ethics, consumer protection, and data privacy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for recognizing and understanding predatory advertising: what makes advertising 'predatory', the vulnerabilities it exploits, the deceptive tactics used, data/algorithmic practices that enable it, common industry examples, and regulatory responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predatory advertising (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Predatory advertising, or predatory marketing, is the practice of manipulating vulnerable persons such as children, or adults with cognitive issues into unfavorable market transactions through the undisclosed exploitation of these vulnerabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that vulnerabilities are context-dependent and may not exist across all circumstances; the practice often involves undisclosed exploitation and may rely on false or misleading messaging. Use this definition as the primary threshold for labeling advertising 'predatory' rather than mere targeted marketing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent of the advertiser (distinguishing predatory from ordinary targeting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all marketing or advertisements targeting particular traits are necessarily 'predatory'; the condition for the practice relies primarily on the intent of the advertiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because targeting 'pain points' is common even in ethical marketing, whether conduct is predatory can be opaque and requires assessing if the advertiser deliberately exploits vulnerabilities to coerce asymmetrical transactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain biological or physiological traits render an individual less likely to engage in market transactions from a fair position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: targeting overweight individuals with ineffective weight-loss supplements, advertising unregulated 'medical' devices to people with degenerative or painful diseases. Consider whether the product exploits physical conditions and whether claims are supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive deficiencies render an individual unable to fully comprehend and process advertising information that may be deceptive or manipulative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes cognitively disabled persons and groups like minors or the elderly; assess comprehension capacity and whether the advertising requires understanding the full context to avoid deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivational vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain individual traits or extraordinary personal circumstances inhibit a person's ability to resist or properly negotiate market advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: selling inflated funeral services to freshly grieving individuals (FTC 'Funeral Rule' addresses some practices). Examine timing/context that exploit acute personal circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Social circumstances of an individual greatly increase propensity to engage in unfavorable transactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: marketing for-profit colleges to combat veterans struggling to find employment. Consider social position, community context, and likelihood of limited alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional states—temporary or persistent—are leveraged by advertisers to sell products that purportedly address these emotional ills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With advanced access to personal data, advertisers can deliver ads in near real-time tuned to emotional states. Assess whether messaging exploits grief, fear, shame, loneliness, etc., to drive purchases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual's economic circumstances limit alternatives or increase susceptibility to predatory marketing schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: marketing high-interest payday loans to financially unstable individuals. Look for offers that prey on lack of alternatives, high cost terms, or exploit financial desperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deception tactics (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many predatory advertisers rely on demonstrably false or otherwise deceitful claims, including statements true at face value but relying on omissions or context to mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers classify deceptive tactics to understand their use. Evaluate not only outright falsehoods but also contextual omissions and implications designed to create false inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: False statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims or presentations that are demonstrably false, often statistics or other empirical claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for-profit college claiming '98% of our graduates find employment within one month' when untrue. Verify empirical claims against reliable data sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements about a product/service that fail to include material information relevant to the claim being made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: saying 'clinical trials have proven effectiveness' when the trial measured a different context/metric. Check for missing qualifiers, contexts, sample limitations, or countervailing facts omitted from the ad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication (and subtypes: ambiguous, atypical, conjectural, manipulative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that may be true but are intended to lead consumers to erroneous inferences; can be ambiguous, atypical, conjectural, or manipulative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous: unclear language suggesting superiority without metrics. Atypical: citing unusually good outcomes as typical. Conjectural: claims lacking substantive evidence (e.g., '100% satisfaction guarantee' impossible to ensure). Manipulative: highlighting non-differentiating characteristics to create illusion of superiority (e.g., 'fat-free' soda). Assess whether truthful fragments are used to imply outcomes not supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Collection of personal information through direct submission or inference from user engagement raises informed consent and privacy concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether users gave informed consent, clarity of end-user permissions, and whether data use matches original transaction intent. Note legislative efforts to increase clarity and bounds of data usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data extraction and aggregation / data brokerage
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is gathered from social media, loyalty programs, browser queries, government records, app usage, etc., and aggregated by data brokers into consumer categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for sale or sharing of aggregated profiles (e.g., 'Zero Mobility', 'Credit Crunched: City Families'). Such categorization enables pinpointing and reaching vulnerable groups; evaluate presence of brokered segmentation as indicator of predatory targeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic targeting / micro-targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex algorithms deliver advertisements to individuals based on personal information and inferred characteristics, enabling precise, individualized targeting (micro-targeting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms can increase exposure of vulnerable populations even without malicious intent, by optimizing for engagement; assess whether targeting reinforces vulnerabilities, whether sensitive attributes are inferred, and whether intermediaries (e.g., DoubleClick) are used to place ads across many sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of sensitive attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms and aggregated data can infer traditionally protected information (health, race, private financial histories) without direct collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether inferred sensitive attributes are being used to target ads and whether that inference creates additional risk of predatory exploitation, particularly when consumers cannot detect or consent to such inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intermediaries and ad networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediaries like ad networks relieve individual publishers of ad placement decisions and allow algorithmic matching of ads to users across many sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice can dilute publisher culpability and enable advertisers to reach vulnerable groups through brokered channels; examine ad supply chains and whether platforms monitor placements for exploitative content.

rubrics_metrics.name: For-profit colleges as an example of predatory advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: For-profit institutions have used deceptive marketing targeting low-income individuals and veterans, e.g., misrepresenting enrollment/employment outcomes and leveraging lead generation via data-driven instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for inflated employment claims, targeting of veterans (G.I. Bill beneficiaries), recruitment of emotionally vulnerable individuals, and high rates of student debt with low degree completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predatory lending as an example
rubrics_metrics.description: High-interest loans with unfavorable terms are marketed to financially distressed individuals identified via online behaviors and other data proxies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: ads for payday loans or fringe financial services targeted at users searching coupons/low-paying jobs; presence of 'predatory inclusion' where alternatives are lacking in certain neighborhoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political messaging / micro-targeting risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Micro-targeted political ads tailor messages to individual preferences, concerns, or fears based on personal data, which can harm democratic processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether messages manipulate emotions or exploit vulnerabilities (e.g., Cambridge Analytica scandal). Consider potential for highly inflammatory, personalized political persuasion that bypasses public scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploitation of grieving individuals (funeral industry example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Funeral homes have capitalized on emotional vulnerability by selling unnecessary services or marking up prices; the FTC 'Funeral Rule' requires a 'general price list' to help consumers compare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate timing, transparency of pricing, and presence/absence of mandated disclosures when assessing predatory practices in grief-related markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children/teens targeting (advergames and branded content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Children often cannot recognize persuasive intent; online 'advergames' use branded characters and reward mechanisms to foster brand preference and influence consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether games integrate branded content as reward mechanics, whether they obscure commercial intent, and potential links to poor health outcomes (e.g., exposure to low-nutrient food advertising).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative and regulatory approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses include FTC enforcement and legislative proposals aiming at notice, opt-out, limits on data retention, access to consumer data, and restrictions on operational uses of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of proposed but not passed bills: Consumer Privacy Protection Act (notice of unrelated uses; opt-out for up to five years), Commercial Privacy Bill of Rights (notice, opt-out for behavioral advertising, remedies for inaccuracies), Data Broker Accountability and Transparency Act (access to collected information). Note debates: transparency alone may be insufficient; some advocate direct limits on data use while opponents warn of hampering beneficial uses.
